key_insight: When many employers rely on screening algorithms from a single vendor, outcomes become correlated and produce systematic racial disparities—certain individuals and racial groups face concentrated rejection risk.
problem_solved: Quantifies and exposes the harms of vendor-level algorithmic monoculture in hiring: how single-vendor dominance can create correlated, inequitable screening outcomes across many employers.
method: Assembled a novel dataset of ~3 million applicants and ~4 million applications all screened by the same algorithm vendor.
Performed statistical comparisons of screening outcomes by race with robustness checks (covariate controls, subgroup/intersectional analyses).
Assessed vendor-level effects via correlation analyses and counterfactual/robustness experiments to isolate monoculture-driven disparities.
impact: Shows that vendor concentration is a systemic fairness risk—practitioners should audit vendor models, diversify screening pipelines, and monitor vendor-level metrics when procuring hiring algorithms.
visual_elements: Sankey/flow diagram: applicants → vendor screening → hire/reject, colored by race to show concentrated rejections
Grouped bar chart: rejection/advancement rates by racial group (with confidence intervals)
Network map: employers connected to a dominant vendor to visualize monoculture reach
Heatmap or correlation matrix: similarity of outcomes across employers indicating monoculture-driven alignment
paper_authors: Rishi Bommasani, Sarah H. Bana, Kathleen A. Creel, Dan Jurafsky, Percy Liang
